opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it mostly comes down to efficiency, and to what you actually want the model to spend its capacity on.

If you patchify directly in pixel space, you inherit the full dimensionality of the image. A 512 by 512 RGB image is close to 800,000 values. With reasonably small patches you get a very long token sequence, and since attention scales quadratically with sequence length, compute and memory blow up fast. You can use bigger patches to shorten the sequence, but then each token carries a huge, highly redundant chunk of raw pixels. The model ends up spending much of its capacity on high-frequency detail and local correlations that aren't really semantically interesting.

A good autoencoder, whether a VAE or something similar, has already done much of that perceptual compression for you. It squeezes out the redundancy and keeps a compact representation that still preserves what matters for reconstruction. Typically you downsample spatially by a factor of eight or so, with a modest number of channels. When you then patchify that latent, each token already summarizes a meaningful region of the image, and your sequence is dramatically shorter. The transformer or diffusion backbone can focus on the hard part, which is global structure, composition, and semantics, instead of relearning low-level image statistics.

There's also a nice separation of concerns. The autoencoder handles fidelity, textures, and fine detail. The generative model handles modeling the distribution over images at a more abstract level. You can train and improve those pieces somewhat independently. Empirically, that division gives you better quality per FLOP, faster training, and much more practical inference at high resolution.

That said, it isn't free. You're bounded by the quality of the autoencoder. If the latent space loses information, small text, fine faces, or crisp edges, the generator can't recover it. And the latent space has its own geometry, so how well it's regularized affects how easy it is to model. So there's real ongoing work on designing better latent spaces and tokenizers, and some people are revisiting pixel-space approaches with smarter architectures. But for the compute budgets most of us work with, latent-space patchification is the sweet spot.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the short answer is efficiency, but there's a little more to it than that. If you think about a high-resolution image, say 1024 by 1024, and you try to patchify that directly in pixel space, you end up with an enormous number of tokens for a transformer to attend over. Attention is quadratic in sequence length, so the compute just explodes. You can use bigger patches to keep the token count manageable, but then each patch is swallowing a lot of raw pixel detail, and the model has to learn to reconstruct fine texture from a very coarse grid. That's a hard job.

Latent space fixes a lot of that. When you first pass the image through an autoencoder, you're compressing it, typically eight times in each spatial dimension, so you get a representation that's sixty-four times smaller in area. And crucially, the autoencoder has already done the work of throwing away perceptually irrelevant information. Natural images are very redundant at the pixel level, neighboring pixels are highly correlated, and the latent captures the semantically meaningful structure while discarding the noise. So when you patchify on top of that, each token is already carrying a much richer, more abstract piece of content. The diffusion or flow model can spend its capacity on composition, layout, semantics, rather than on learning low-level statistics that a VAE handles perfectly well on its own.

There's also a nice practical benefit on the training side. The latent is smoother and better behaved than raw pixels, so the denoising objective is easier to optimize, and you converge faster. And because the autoencoder decoder is doing the final upsampling, you get sharp outputs without the transformer needing to predict every pixel explicitly.

Now, it's not free. You inherit whatever limitations the autoencoder has, so if the latent space is lossy in certain ways, text rendering or fine details, for example, the generative model can never recover that. So the quality of the autoencoder becomes a first-class concern. But on balance, for image generation at the resolutions people actually want, working in latent space and patchifying there is a much better trade-off than trying to do it in pixel space.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is efficiency. An image in pixel space contains a lot of redundancy. If you divide it into small patches, you get a long sequence of tokens, which makes the transformer expensive to run. If you make the patches larger, you shorten the sequence, but each token has to represent much more raw information.

In latent space, an encoder has already compressed the image into a more compact representation. So when we patchify that representation, the transformer can work with fewer tokens and focus on modeling the structure and content of the image. The decoder then maps the generated representation back into pixels.

There is a tradeoff, though. Anything the encoder discards is information the generative model cannot directly recover. So the quality of that latent representation matters. But with a good encoder and decoder, it gives us a useful balance between computational cost and image quality.

sol-6.1.text:
The main advantage is efficiency. Images have a lot of redundancy in pixel space, so if you patchify the original image, you either end up with a very long sequence of tokens or you use large patches and lose fine detail. A long sequence is particularly expensive for a transformer because the cost of attention grows quadratically with the number of tokens.

In latent space, an encoder has already compressed the image into a much smaller representation. We can patchify that representation and let the generative model work with fewer tokens while still preserving the information needed to reconstruct the image. The decoder then maps the generated latents back into pixels.

There is a tradeoff, of course: anything the encoder loses, the generative model cannot recover faithfully. But with a good latent representation, we get a very useful balance between computational cost and image quality.
